details:
**Lions' den**
Daniel's most famous story (chapter 6). Jealous officials persuade King Darius the Mede to sign a decree that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or man except the king. Daniel keeps praying toward Jerusalem three times a day and is thrown into a den of lions, but God sends an angel to shut the lions' mouths, and he emerges unharmed the next morning.

**Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the fiery furnace**
Daniel's three companions, whose Hebrew names are Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. They refuse to bow to a golden statue sixty cubits high and six cubits wide set up by Nebuchadnezzar, so they are thrown into a blazing furnace. They walk out unharmed, and a fourth figure "like a son of the gods" is seen in the flames with them. The Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Holy Children are Greek additions to this episode.

**Writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast**
During a feast where the Babylonian king Belshazzar drinks from vessels looted from the Jerusalem Temple, a disembodied hand writes "Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin" on the palace wall. Belshazzar promises purple clothing, a gold chain, and the rank of third ruler in the kingdom to whoever can read it. Daniel explains that the kingdom has been numbered, weighed, and divided, and Belshazzar is slain that night as Darius the Mede takes the kingdom.

**Statue of four metals with feet of clay**
Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great statue with a head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with clay. A stone cut without hands smashes it and grows into a mountain. Daniel interprets the metals as four successive kingdoms that God's eternal kingdom will replace, and the dream is the source of the phrase "feet of clay."

**Vegetables and water for ten days**
At the Babylonian court, Daniel and his friends refuse the king's rich food and wine and request only pulse (vegetables) and water. After ten days they look healthier ("fairer and fatter") than the other youths, and they are later found "ten times better" than all the king's magicians and enchanters.

**Bel and the Dragon**
A deuterocanonical addition to Daniel found in Greek versions. Daniel solves a locked-room mystery by scattering ashes on the temple floor, whose footprints show that the priests of the idol Bel, not the idol, were secretly eating its offerings. He then kills a sacred dragon by feeding it cakes of pitch, fat, and hair, which make it burst, and he is again thrown to the lions and survives.

**Susanna and the Elders**
Another deuterocanonical addition, included in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Two lecherous elders spy on the virtuous Susanna as she bathes and falsely accuse her of adultery when she refuses them. The young Daniel questions them separately and exposes their lie when they name different trees under which the act supposedly happened, and the elders are put to death.

**Ram and goat vision**
In chapter 8, Daniel sees a two-horned ram (Media and Persia) destroyed by a goat with one great horn (Greece, with the horn representing Alexander the Great). The horn breaks and is replaced by four horns, representing the division of Alexander's empire, and Daniel is told the sanctuary will afterward be cleansed.

**Four beasts from the sea**
In chapter 7, Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea: a winged lion, a bear with three ribs in its mouth, a four-headed leopard with wings, and a terrifying beast with great iron teeth and ten horns, from which grows a little horn that speaks boastfully. The "Ancient of Days" sits in judgment and gives everlasting dominion to "one like a son of man."

**Nebuchadnezzar's tree dream and madness**
Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree that shelters every animal and from which "all flesh was fed," until it is cut down to a stump. Daniel explains that the tree is the king himself, who then goes mad for seven years ("seven times"), living in the wild and eating grass like an ox until he acknowledges God.

**Seventy weeks prophecy**
In chapter 9, while reflecting on Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years of desolation for Jerusalem, Daniel is told by the angel Gabriel that "seventy weeks" (seventy sevens) are decreed. They are divided into seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, after which "an anointed one shall be cut off," a passage many Christians read as a prophecy of Christ.

**Belteshazzar**
The Babylonian name given to Daniel at Nebuchadnezzar's court, where he becomes chief of the magicians. It should not be confused with Belshazzar, the king at the feast. The Hebrew name Daniel means "God is my judge."

**Antiochus IV Epiphanes**
Modern scholars generally date the composition of Daniel to around 165 BCE, during the persecution of the Jews by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV. His desecration of the Jerusalem Temple is widely seen as the subject of the book's later visions, including the "little horn."

**Michael and the prince of Persia**
In chapter 10, a heavenly man with a body like beryl (or topaz) and a face like lightning appears to Daniel. He explains that he was delayed by the "prince of Persia," a hostile angelic power, until the archangel Michael came to help him.

**Kings of the north and south and "time, times, and half a time"**
Daniel's final visions (chapters 11–12) describe wars between the "king of the north" and the "king of the south," generally identified with the Seleucid and Ptolemaic dynasties. They predict a period of "a time, times, and half a time," a phrase central to later end-times calculations such as the 1,260-day prophecy, and promise that the wise "shall shine like the stars for ever and ever."
